title: I taught Ephraim to walk (Hosea 11:1–4)
hook: God as a parent holding a toddler's hands, bending down to feed

segments.voice: Yesterday, Darius and the lions' den, and Daniel's open window. Your line: the window stays open.

Watch a parent teach a toddler to walk. They crouch behind the child, one finger in each tiny fist, bent nearly double, back aching. The child has no idea anyone is holding on, thinks they're walking all alone, and that's the point. Later, the same parent leans down with a spoon, patient, while half of it lands on the floor. Somebody probably held each of us like that once, and nobody remembers it. An old prophet named Hosea reached for exactly this picture of God. Not a king on a throne. A parent on their knees in the hallway.

Hosea preached in the northern kingdom of Israel, and his book often calls the north Ephraim, after one of its tribes. In the King James Bible: "When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt." The Exodus, remembered not as a battle but as a parent calling a child home. Then the toddler scene: "I taught Ephraim also to go, taking them by their arms; but they knew not that I healed them." That's the ache: held, fed and healed, and never noticed. Verse four: "I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love." Not chains for an animal. Human cords, the kind a person uses to guide someone they love. Then a farmer's picture: God easing the yoke off their jaws and bending down to lay food before them. The chapter isn't sweet all the way through. Hosea names the people's turning away, and hard years coming. But a few verses later God says, in effect, my heart is turned within me; I can't give you up. The love outlasts the anger. Matthew's Gospel later borrows the first line, out of Egypt have I called my son, and hears it in the child Jesus and his family in Egypt. Christians who follow Matthew hear Hosea on two levels: Israel's story, and a pattern Jesus walks again. Either way, God in this book is the one on their knees.
screen: `OUT OF EGYPT: A PARENT CALLING HOME.`
`CORDS OF A MAN, BANDS OF LOVE.`
then, large: `I TAUGHT EPHRAIM ALSO TO GO.`

segments.voice: Picture the hands of someone who held you up before you could stand, even if you don't remember it; Hosea's point is that you probably wouldn't. Then think of a small one in your life now, a child, a pet, a seedling, a younger colleague finding their feet, and one small act of care you could give them. If you pray, give thanks for the hands that held you; if not, simply let the gratitude sit.
Ahavah. Hebrew for love: the cords Hosea says God used to draw a people, like a parent holding a toddler's arms, feeding them, healing them unseen.
Your line: cords of love. Most of the holding goes unseen, even by the one being held. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians read Hosea 11 in sermons and Bible study as a picture of God's parental love, and Matthew 2:15 quotes its first verse in the story of Jesus' childhood.

notes: The index word/title says 'to walk'; the KJV reads 'to go'. The script explains this. Consider whether the title should stay modern.
Dating Hosea to roughly 700 years before Jesus (he prophesied in the 8th century BC, before the fall of Samaria in 722 BC). Confirm the phrasing.
Verse 4's yoke/feeding picture is paraphrased; translations differ on whether the image is an infant lifted to the cheek or an ox's yoke. The KJV supports the yoke reading. Confirm.
Hosea 11:8 ('mine heart is turned within me') is paraphrased, not quoted. Confirm 'how can I give you up' paraphrase is fair.
Typological reading of Matthew 2:15 described as common among Christians, not ranked against other readings.
